metadata.title: Sample Course Descriptions — Bachelor of Science in Software Engineering (BSSE)
metadata.programme: Bachelor of Science in Software Engineering (BSSE)
metadata.department: Department of Networks, School of Computing and Informatics Technology (SCIT)
metadata.college: College of Computing and Information Sciences (CoCIS)
metadata.provenance: Synthetic — created by Imaan (Quality/Security Lead) for the RAG corpus. Course structures are consistent with the BSSE programme overview and academic calendar already in the corpus. Individual course details are representative samples, not verbatim excerpts from an official catalogue.
metadata.use: Enables the Student-Support Case Agent to answer questions about specific course units, credit loads, prerequisites, and year of study.

courses.title: Introduction to Software Engineering
courses.prerequisites: None — open to all Year 1 BSSE students
courses.description: Introduces the discipline of software engineering: its history, motivation, and scope. Topics include the software development lifecycle (SDLC), software process models (waterfall, agile, spiral), roles in a software team, and an overview of software quality. Students complete a small team-based exercise applying a chosen process model.
courses.assessment: Coursework 40% (assignments and group exercise), Final examination 60%

courses.title: Programming Fundamentals
courses.description: Covers the foundational concepts of programming using Python. Topics include variables and data types, control flow (conditionals, loops), functions, basic data structures (lists, dictionaries), file I/O, and an introduction to object-oriented concepts. Laboratory sessions reinforce each concept through guided coding exercises.
courses.assessment: Coursework 40% (lab exercises and assignments), Final examination 60%

courses.title: Object-Oriented Programming
courses.description: Deepens programming skills with a focus on object-oriented design and implementation in Java. Topics include classes and objects, encapsulation, inheritance, polymorphism, interfaces, exception handling, and basic design patterns. Students develop a mid-sized object-oriented application as a semester project.

courses.title: Database Systems
courses.description: Covers the design and use of relational database systems. Topics include the Entity-Relationship (ER) model, relational algebra, SQL (DDL and DML), normalisation (1NF–3NF/BCNF), transaction management, concurrency control, and an introduction to NoSQL databases. Lab sessions use MySQL.
courses.assessment: Coursework 40% (SQL assignments and database design project), Final examination 60%

courses.title: Software Architecture and Design
courses.description: Examines the principles and practices of designing large-scale software systems. Topics include architectural styles (layered, microservices, event-driven, pipe-and-filter), design patterns (GoF patterns), UML modelling, quality attributes (scalability, maintainability, security), and architectural evaluation methods. Students produce a documented architecture for a realistic case study.
courses.assessment: Coursework 50% (design assignments and architecture document), Final examination 50%

courses.title: Research Methods in Software Engineering
courses.prerequisites: BSE2201 Object-Oriented Programming, BSE2205 Database Systems
courses.description: Prepares students for final-year research and project work. Topics include formulating research questions, literature review methodology, quantitative and qualitative research approaches, ethical considerations in computing research, academic writing and citation, and an introduction to research tools (LaTeX, reference managers). Students submit a research proposal.
courses.assessment: Coursework 60% (literature review and research proposal), Final examination 40%

courses.title: Advanced Software Engineering
courses.description: Builds on core software engineering with advanced topics: agile at scale (SAFe, LeSS), DevOps and continuous delivery pipelines, software measurement and metrics, formal methods and specifications, software security engineering, and the economics of software projects (cost estimation, ROI). Students conduct a case study of a real-world engineering failure.
courses.assessment: Coursework 50% (case study report and assignments), Final examination 50%

courses.title: Final Year Project I
courses.prerequisites: BSE3105 Research Methods in Software Engineering — students must have submitted and received feedback on their research proposal
courses.description: First half of the two-semester capstone project. Students work individually or in pairs, under a supervisor, to define a software engineering problem, conduct a detailed literature review, design a solution, and produce a project proposal document and an initial prototype. Weekly supervision meetings are required.
courses.assessment: Continuous assessment 100% (proposal document 40%, prototype demo 40%, supervision attendance 20%)

courses.title: Final Year Project II
courses.prerequisites: BSE4101 Final Year Project I — a pass in Project I is required before proceeding
courses.description: Completion of the capstone project. Students implement, test, and evaluate their solution, then write a full project report and present their work to a panel of examiners. The final report must include background, methodology, results, discussion, and conclusion chapters, and must meet the department's formatting and citation standards.
courses.assessment: Continuous assessment 100% (final report 50%, oral presentation and defence 40%, supervision attendance 10%)

courses.title: Emerging Trends in Software Engineering
courses.prerequisites: BSE3101 Software Architecture and Design, BSE3203 Advanced Software Engineering, BSE3105 Research Methods in Software Engineering
courses.description: Surveys recent and emerging developments that are reshaping software engineering practice. Topics covered in 2026/2027 include: AI-assisted software development (GitHub Copilot, LLM-driven testing), agentic AI systems and their engineering challenges, large language models (LLMs) as components in software systems, responsible AI and ethics in software products, low-code/no-code platforms, WebAssembly and edge computing, and quantum computing fundamentals for software engineers. Each topic is examined through both a technical lens and a professional/ethical lens. Students complete a research review and a small proof-of-concept project on a topic of their choice.
courses.assessment: Coursework 60% (research review 30%, proof-of-concept project and demo 30%), Final examination 40%
